analysis.one_liner: Automatically enrolls workers without a workplace retirement plan into low-cost pooled funds that pay lifetime annuities.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to its retirement-policy committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup, hearing, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require employers that don't offer a retirement plan to give workers access to a USA Retirement Fund, with payroll savings automatically deducted unless the worker opts out. The money would go into professionally managed, trustee-governed funds and pay out as a lifetime monthly income in old age, instead of a lump sum that has to be stretched over a retirement. It also bundles a series of smaller protections: limits on hidden rollover sales tactics, statements that show a 401(k) balance as monthly retirement income, rules for small-employer plans, and changes to the federal pension insurance program.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers offer no retirement plan — a group that skews toward lower-wage and small-business jobs — get an automatic, low-cost savings channel with lifetime income, without needing to sign up on their own. Employees at companies with weak plans also benefit if their plan lacks lifetime income options, because those plans wouldn't count as qualifying. Pooled plan providers and asset managers gain a new institutional market for managing these funds.

how_it_helps.text: Employers that don't maintain a qualifying plan must make an automatic USA Retirement Fund arrangement available to each qualifying employee, with payroll deductions treated as elected unless the worker opts out.
The default contribution ramps from 3 percent of pay in 2015 to 6 percent of pay after 2017, and a worker who opts out is re-enrolled after two years absent a new election.
Each Fund must pay benefits in the form of an annuity, providing a stream of income for life, with joint-and-survivor protections for spouses.

Fund trustees must be independent of service providers, and the bill gives participants petition rights, disclosure of fees and performance, and a vote (non-binding) on trustee compensation at funds with over $250 million in assets.

Employers are not treated as fiduciaries merely for making the Fund available, limiting their legal exposure while still holding them responsible for enrollment and timely transmission of contributions.

The bill requires pension benefit statements to illustrate a participant's balance as an estimated lifetime income stream, and provides a fiduciary safe harbor for selecting an insurer for lifetime income contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers take on new administrative duties — enrolling employees, remitting contributions on time, and paying civil penalties of $100 per employee per year for failing to offer the arrangement. Retail investment advisors and broker-dealers who earn commissions selling lump-sum rollovers would lose business, since the bill states that rollover advice combined with investment recommendations counts as fiduciary investment advice. Workers bear reduced access to cash: distributions are largely restricted to annuity payments, with only limited one-time withdrawals before or after age 60.

drawbacks.text: Automatic enrollment means money is deducted from a worker's paycheck by default, and an election to stop contributing expires after two years, after which the worker is re-enrolled unless they opt out again — money some low-income workers may need for current expenses.

USA Retirement Fund annuity payments may be adjusted downward to reflect the Fund's experience to protect its finances, up to 5 percent per year for those already receiving payments, so the lifetime income is not fixed the way a traditional pension benefit is.

Covered employers face a civil money penalty of $100 per employee per year for failing to provide the arrangement, plus enforcement actions if they fail to remit contributions on time, a real compliance cost for small businesses just above the 10-employee exception.

The bill restricts withdrawals: except for limited one-time distributions of $5,500 before age 60 or up to $10,000 or half the benefit after 60, participants can only take their money as an annuity, so savings are not available for emergencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but weighted toward workers: automatic enrollment with lifetime-income payout addresses the two biggest failures of the current voluntary 401(k) system — people who never sign up, and balances that run out because they aren't annuitized. The cost side is modest for employers (compliance duties and penalties, offset by a broad liability shield) and the payout can drift downward with fund experience, but the bill builds in disclosure, actuarial certification of any cuts, and participant governance rights. The bundle of retirement-industry provisions — annuity safe harbors and pooled-plan structures — is secondary and mostly extends existing law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin, with Senator Sherrod Brown, introduced the bill on January 30, 2014.
Three Democratic senators cosponsored it; no Republican did.

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day — the complete action history contains no other action, no hearing or markup, and no vote.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill was never taken up again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed. Workers without a workplace retirement plan gained nothing, while employers avoided new enrollment and remittance duties and retail retirement advisors kept selling lump-sum rollovers without the bill's fiduciary restrictions. The existing 401(k) and IRA market stayed as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and retail advisors; status quo held

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without a vote, so no roll-call ever measured party positions.

industries.industry: Pooled plan providers and asset managers
industries.note: The bill would route automatic payroll savings from millions of uncovered workers into professionally managed USA Retirement Funds, creating a large new institutional management market. The funds' low-fee, independent-trustee structure is designed to serve workers, so the industry's gain runs alongside the public benefit.

The bill states that advising a participant to take a lump-sum distribution combined with a recommendation on how to invest it counts as fiduciary investment advice, which curbs conflicted rollover sales. That restriction aligns the industry's loss with worker protection.

Lifetime-income disclosures, a fiduciary safe harbor for selecting insurers for annuity contracts, and a clarification that annuity features don't disqualify a default investment would expand annuity sales. Workers gain the lifetime-income protections these provisions support, but insurers gain the business.

Covered employers must make the arrangement available, remit contributions on time, and face civil penalties for failures — but they are shielded from fiduciary liability for the Fund itself and exempt if they have 10 or fewer qualifying employees. Their compliance cost is the flip side of the worker benefit.
